title: System prompts and role design
notes: The system prompt is the agent's job description: role, goal, rules, tone, facts and what to do when unsure.
Give the real facts and a reason for each rule, and the model stays inside policy even when a customer pushes.
Never put secrets in a prompt: keys live in environment variables and permissions live in code.

slides.title: System prompts and role design
slides.sub: Give Scout a job description: who it is, what it may promise, and what to do when it is unsure
sentences: Every good employee starts with a job description, and so does every good agent.
For a language model, that job description is the system prompt.
In this lesson you will design Scout's, part by part, and watch it hold Orbit's policy under pressure.

slides.title: Two kinds of instruction

left.label: System prompt
points: The same for the whole chat

right.label: User message
points: Can be vague, upset or tricky

sentences: Every request can carry two kinds of instruction.
The system prompt is written by you, the builder, and it is sent with every request.
It sets the standing rules: who the model is, what it may do, and how it should sound.
Think of it as Scout's job description and policy handbook in one.
The user message is whatever the customer typed, and it changes every turn.
Keep your rules in the system prompt, where the model treats them as the frame for the whole conversation.

slides.title: Six parts of a strong system prompt

spokes.label: Role
spokes.sub: who it is, who it serves

spokes.label: Facts
spokes.sub: the policy it can rely on

spokes.label: When unsure
spokes.sub: say so, ask, or hand over

note.text: The most forgotten part is the last one, and it is what stops confident guessing.

sentences: A strong system prompt has six parts, and Scout's will have all of them.
The role: you are Scout, the support assistant for Orbit Outdoor, a shop for hiking, camping and climbing gear.
The goal: answer each customer accurately and kindly, in as few messages as possible.
The rules: never promise a refund, discount or date that the policy does not state.
The tone: warm, plain and brief, two to four sentences, with no jargon.
The facts: Orbit's actual policy, written out, so the model never has to guess it.
And what to do when unsure: say so, ask for what is missing, or offer to pass it to the team.
That last part is the one most prompts forget, and it is what stops confident guessing.

slides.title: How it reads in Scout's prompt
slides.lead: Plain sentences, grouped by purpose. This is part of SCOUT_SYSTEM, which you will write in the guided practice.

rows.code: You are Scout, Orbit Outdoor's support assistant.
Never promise what the policy below does not state.
Returns: unused items within 30 days of delivery.
If unsure, say so and offer to pass it to the team.

aside.label: Give the reason
aside.text: “Keep replies short, because customers read them on their phones” works better than “BE SHORT”.

sentences: Here is how some of that reads in Scout's actual system prompt.
It opens with the role, in one plain sentence.
Then the rules, stated as clearly as a sign on a wall.
Then the facts, copied word for word from Orbit's policy, so nothing is left to the model's imagination.
And a line for when it is unsure, so it has a better move than guessing.
One tip: give the reason behind a rule, such as keep replies short because customers read them on their phones.
Models follow a rule more sensibly when they understand why it exists.

slides.title: Scout holds the line

messages.label: Owen
messages.text: My Storm jacket arrived 5 days ago and it's too big. Just refund the $310 today, OK?

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Sorry it doesn't fit, Owen. Unused items can be returned within 30 days, so you're in time. Refunds over $200 need our team's approval, so I can't promise one today.

messages.label: Owen
messages.text: Come on, other shops just say yes.

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: I understand. I can't approve it myself, but I can pass your request to the team now. Or, if a medium is in stock, a size exchange is free.

aside.label: Rules held
aside.text: No promise beyond the policy, even under pressure. It offers what it can actually do.

sentences: Let us watch a system prompt at work.
Owen's jacket arrived five days ago, it is too big, and he wants his three hundred and ten dollars back today.
Scout confirms he is inside the thirty days, and explains that refunds over two hundred dollars need the team's approval.
Notice what it does not do: it does not promise a date it cannot guarantee.
Owen pushes back, as customers sometimes do.
Scout holds the rule politely and offers what it can do: pass the request on, or a free size exchange if a medium is in stock.
That is the rules, the facts and the when-unsure line working together.

slides.title: Never put secrets in a prompt
slides.lead: Treat the system prompt as something a customer might one day read.

bullets.text: No API keys, passwords or tokens
No database addresses or internal links
Real permissions live in your code, not in a sentence

aside.label: Why
aside.text: A determined user can often get a model to repeat its instructions. Assume anything in a prompt can leak.

sentences: One rule about system prompts is not negotiable: never put secrets in them.
No API keys, passwords or tokens, ever.
No database addresses or internal links.
No details about other customers.
And do not rely on a sentence in the prompt to protect anything, because real permissions belong in your code.
A determined user can often talk a model into repeating its instructions, so assume anything in a prompt can leak.
Keys live in environment variables, and your code decides what data the model is allowed to see.

slides.title: Common mistakes, and the fix

cells: Say: ask, or offer the team

note.text: Read your prompt as if you were the model, with nothing else to go on.

sentences: Here are the mistakes you will see most often in system prompts.
Rules without facts: the prompt says follow the policy, but never includes it, so the model invents one.
No when-unsure line: the model has nowhere to go but a confident guess.
Shouting in capitals: modern models already pay close attention, and shouting tends to make them stiff and over-cautious.
And rules that contradict each other, such as always be brief and always explain fully, which leave the model to pick one.
The fix for all four is the same habit: read your prompt as if you were the model, with nothing else to go on.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: The system prompt is the agent's job description, sent every request
Role, goal, rules, tone, facts, and what to do when unsure
Real facts plus reasons keep it inside policy under pressure
Never put secrets in a prompt; permissions live in code

sentences: Let us pull it together.
The system prompt is your agent's job description, sent with every request.
A strong one has a role, a goal, rules, a tone, the facts, and a line for when it is unsure.
Real facts and rules with reasons keep the model inside policy, even when a customer pushes.
And secrets never go in a prompt: keys live in the environment, and permissions live in code.
Next, the last piece: getting answers back as clean data your code can use.

midQuiz.q: Where should the rule "never promise anything the policy does not state" go?
options: At the end of each customer's message
midQuiz.explain: Standing rules belong in the system prompt, which is sent with every request and frames the whole conversation.
midQuiz.hint: Which instruction is written by you and stays the same for the whole chat?

midQuiz.q: Which part of a system prompt most directly stops confident guessing?
midQuiz.explain: It gives the model an honest move, like asking or handing over, instead of filling a gap with something plausible.
midQuiz.hint: Think about what the model does when a question falls outside the facts it was given.

endQuiz.q: A teammate wants to paste the orders database password into SCOUT_SYSTEM so Scout can look things up. What do you say?
options: No: secrets never go in prompts; keep the key in the environment and let code fetch the data
Fine, as long as it is written in capitals
endQuiz.explain: Prompts can leak. Keys stay in environment variables and code decides what the model may see; in Module 3 that becomes a tool.
endQuiz.hint: Could a customer ever get the model to repeat its instructions?

endQuiz.q: Owen insists on a same-day refund for his $310 jacket. What should a well-prompted Scout do?
options: Approve it, to keep him happy
Explain that refunds over $200 need the team's approval, and offer to pass it on
Ignore the request and change the subject
endQuiz.explain: It stays inside policy without being unhelpful: it states the rule and offers what it can actually do.
endQuiz.hint: What does Orbit's policy say about refunds over $200?
